title: Millennia of Stability, Decades of Change: Tracing 5000 Years of Marine Biodiversity Shifts in the Red Sea
content:
ABSTRACT

Aim

The Red Sea's steep natural gradients in temperature, salinity and turbidity make it an ideal natural laboratory, yet its long-term biodiversity history and sensitivity to human pressures remain poorly resolved. We reconstruct millennial-scale trajectories of marine eukaryotic communities and evaluate how diversity and community composition have changed through time across the basin.

Location

Red Sea, with seven dated sediment cores at 700–2200 m depth.

Time Period

~3200 BCE—2010 CE, encompassing the mid-to-late Holocene.

Major Taxa Studied

Broad marine eukaryote assemblages captured by two universal metabarcoding markers.

Methods

We combined sedimentary ancient DNA (sedaDNA) metabarcoding (18S v7, COI) with radiocarbon (14C) geochronologies across 175 sediment core layer samples. Temporal change and regional structure were assessed using diversity and Ecological Trajectory Analyses and community variation was tested among four biogeochemical proxy bands derived from our core biogeochemistry: productivity, terrigenous input, redox and anthropogenic influence.

Results

Reconstructed communities reveal a diverse system with marked regional differences in community composition across ~5200 years. Ecological trajectory analyses show a long, stable baseline in all zones followed by a recent departure towards the present: strong and distinct in the northern Red Sea, slower but persistent in the central Red Sea and least expressed in the southern Red Sea, though its shorter single-core record limits the comparison. Analysis of biogeochemical data corroborated this departure, localizing it to the post-1800 CE window of time, coinciding in a rise of redox-sensitive and anthropogenic metal signals (significant for 18S v7, marginal trend in COI) and a decline in arthropod and an increase in cnidarian relative abundance.

Main Conclusion

Coupling sedaDNA with geochronology and paleo-biogeochemical evidence provides millennial-scale baselines and reveals region-specific restructuring of the Red Sea's eukaryotic communities coincident with industrial-era environmental change. These findings reinforce the Red Sea's value as a natural laboratory and highlight the urgency of conserving an ecosystem now departing from its long-term historical range.
